title: Windows, glazing and visible interior depth for the Prairie Avenue 1904 programme (package K06, the kit)
status: Built to. The 1808 exemplar (keith_house_1808_prairie, T-2298) is glazed from this file and this generator: its 26 sashes are sash_2over2_flat and its two basement lights area_light without the well, each at its record's own clear size (form.window_kit), replacing the K01 proof's single-plane sash. No other house is glazed from the kit yet.
rule: A window is a true aperture, never a painted panel: a hole through its wall, a reveal on every edge of the hole, a frame, one or two sashes each in its own plane, glass set inside its sash, a blind and curtain edges behind the innermost glass, and a dark enclosed interior behind all of it. Every part is placed by the DEPTH ORDER below, and the glass is the ONLY transparent surface, one layer per light, so no view sorts one transparency against another and no ray through a pane reaches the sky. The parts' sizes are data here and the generator reads them; the check (tools/check_window_kit.py) rebuilds every variant and holds the built geometry to this file.

depth_order._doc: Metres behind the wall's outer face (component frame: +Z out of the wall, so a depth d is z = -d). Each stage must be strictly deeper than the one before it in the BUILT mesh; the check measures it per opening.
depth_order.rule: reveal_depth_m (outer face to frame face) never exceeds the host wall's thickness_m; the backing stands at least backing_depth_m behind the innermost glass and closes the whole outline of the hole.

host_wall.rule_source: RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md section Starting ranges: Solid exterior wall / reveal
host_wall.note: The specimen wall: a 0.36 m masonry wall, the 1808 exemplar's stone front, inside the K01 masonry range. A house's own wall thickness replaces it, and the reveal follows.

parts._doc: The working sizes every variant starts from. A variant may override any of them under its own `overrides`, inside the same range.

reveal_depth_m.note: Outer face to the frame face: a masonry wall's outer leaf, so the sash sits about a brick back and the jamb casts a shadow across the glass in a raking light.

frame.note: The box frame's exposed face inside the reveal (the blind stop and pulley stile together) and how far it runs back. One ring, the sash's housing.

sash.note: A 1 3/4 in sash, two inch stiles, the bottom rail deeper than the top, a check meeting rail of 1 1/4 in on each sash. In a double-hung pair the upper sash runs in the outer track and the lower in the inner, a parting bead between them, so the two sashes and their glass stand in two planes and the meeting rails overlap.

muntin.note: A 7/8 in moulded bar. Panes in one sash are equal: the bars divide the sash's daylight evenly.

glass.note: Glass set 5/8 in into its sash behind the putty line. Drawn as ONE thin transparent layer whose low alpha lets the blind, curtain and dark room read through it, and whose low roughness takes the sky's reflection. Crown and cylinder glass's waviness is not modelled.

blind.note: A holland roller blind behind the inner sash, drawn to a seeded fraction of the daylight height (two neighbouring windows rarely agree), with a wooden lath at its foot. Cream holland is the working colour; green and buff were as usual.

curtain.note: A curtain edge at each side of the daylight, behind the blind, folded so a raking light finds its pleats. The colour is a dark red damask's; it is a reconstruction a house's interior evidence replaces.

backing.note: The room behind the glass: the hole's outline carried back three quarters of a metre and capped, in a dark warm finish, so an oblique view sees a recess with sides and a back, never sky, and never a black plane on the glass.

sill.note: A stone sill weathered to fall outward 12 mm over its depth, projecting 50 mm beyond the face, with horns built 80 mm into the jambs either side and a throated drip under its nose so water leaves the sill before it reaches the wall.

head_band.note: The head's dressing: a flat lintel over a flat head, an arch band following a segmental, round or pointed head from spring to spring. Its voussoirs, keystone and stone are K02's (T-2289); this is the band's envelope only.

well.note: The area well a basement light sits in: a box below grade wider than the light by a side margin each way, its floor below the sill, its walls capped with a coping flush above grade.

arch._doc: A head's arch is set by its spring (the height the curve starts from) and its rise above the spring. The check holds each kind to its own geometry.

round.rise: rise = span / 2 (a semicircle on the spring line)

pointed.rise: rise > span / 2 (equilateral: each arc centred on the opposite jamb, rise = span * sqrt(3) / 2)

ranges._doc: RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md section Starting ranges: Sash proportions, for an undocumented ordinary sash. Grouped windows, basement lights, attic lights and leaded lights are authored individually (the same rule's own words), so a variant marked `ordinary: false` states why and is held to its own clear size instead.
ranges.rule_source: RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md section Starting ranges: Sash proportions

restrictions.why: ASSET-CATALOG.md section K06 asks for 'limited leaded lights'. Leaded quarries are an accent of a stair landing, a transom or an attic light in this district, never a street front's working sash. It binds the leaded lights a reconstruction places: one a photograph shows names that source (pictured_by) and is built where the picture puts it (T-3091, 1812 Prairie's small arched window).

costs._doc: Triangle budget per opening, as built. An opening over its budget is refused, so a kit change that bloats every window in the town is caught here, before any house is built from it.

_variants_doc: panes = [columns, rows] of glass in EACH sash (a two-over-two is [2, 1] in each of its two sashes); bays = sashes side by side under one head, divided by mullion_m of masonry; operation names the sashes and fixed lights the opening holds; curtains: false leaves the curtain edges out where a room would not hang them (a basement, an attic, a stair); rise_over_span sets a segmental head's own rise (T-2818), where arch.segmental's working figure is otherwise used.

variants.head: flat
variants.note: The working street sash: double-hung, two lights over two, a flat head under a stone lintel. The commonest form the register's 'regular sash' and 'sash grid' describe.

variants.head: segmental
variants.note: Plate-glass sash, one light over one, under a segmental arch whose upper sash follows the curve: the register's 'paired segmental windows' and 'segmental window hoods' in their single form.

variants.head: round
variants.note: A round-arched opening: a one-over-one sash to the spring, a transom bar on the spring line and a fixed semicircular fanlight above it with radial bars. The register's 'arched windows', the Romanesque rule's 'thick round-arched reveals'.

variants.head: pointed
variants.note: An equilateral pointed head over a two-over-two sash whose upper sash follows both arcs to the point: one of the register's 'pointed twin windows' under a Gothic gable.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two ordinary sashes and a stone mullion under one lintel, authored as a group
variants.note: Two plate-glass sashes either side of a 0.2 m stone mullion under one lintel; each bay's clear width is inside the ordinary range.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a sash with a fixed transom light over it is taller than an ordinary sash by its transom
variants.note: A one-over-one sash under a transom bar and a fixed three-light transom: the sash itself is inside the ordinary range.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a French window: two casement leaves down to the floor they open onto, under a transom, so its clear height is a storey's floor-to-head and not a sash's
variants.note: Two casement leaves meeting at the middle, each glazed in two lights over its bottom rail, under a 0.06 m transom bar and a fixed four-light transom; the leaves stand on the opening's sill, the floor of the balcony they open onto. The shape is 1637 Prairie's engraving's (T-2534: a wide opening to the floor over a balcony, a transom across its head, its leaves meeting on a light middle stile); the glazing bars are the kit's, finer than the engraving resolves.

variants.head: round
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two narrow round-headed lights either side of a stone mullion, authored as a pair under one block of voussoirs
variants.note: Two one-over-one lights, each under its own round head that its upper sash follows, either side of a 0.2 m stone mullion: the upper-storey pairs of 1612 Prairie's photograph (T-2366), which the K01 stone front closes under one block of voussoirs and a keystone.

variants.head: round
variants.why_not_ordinary: a long parlour window: wider than an ordinary sash, two lights a sash across under a semicircular fanlight
variants.note: A tall round-arched parlour window reaching nearly to the floor: a two-light double-hung sash to the spring, a transom bar on the spring line and a fanlight over it. The principal-storey windows of 1612 Prairie's photograph (T-2366).

variants.head: round
variants.why_not_ordinary: a long parlour window: wider than an ordinary sash, two lights a sash across under a round head glazed as a lattice
variants.note: The wide fanlight sash (k06.opening.sash_round_fanlight_wide) with its round head glazed as a grid of square lights between muntins 0.2 m apart, in place of the radial bars: 1623 Prairie's principal window in its 1886 drawing, whose head the pen draws as a lattice of small square panes over a transom on the spring line (T-2819). The bars' pitch is read off the drawing (about eight squares across the 1.8 m head); their section is the kit's muntin.

variants.head: segmental
variants.why_not_ordinary: a long window opening onto a balcony: wider than an ordinary sash, three lights a sash across under a segmental fanlight
variants.note: The wide fanlight sash (k06.opening.sash_round_fanlight_wide) under a flatter, segmental head: a three-light double-hung sash to the spring, a transom bar on the spring line and a fanlight with radial bars over it. The large window over the balcony of 1812 Prairie's photograph (T-2889), whose head the print draws rising about 0.76 m over a 2.8 m span (rise over span 0.27), well short of a round head's half span. T-3091, from the print at 4x (x 430-710, y 470-640 px, 88.5 px a metre): its lights are unequal, the middle one's glass about 120 px (1.36 m) between posts about 17-18 px (0.2 m) and the side ones' about 40 and 43 px (light_ratios 1 : 2.9 : 1, post_m); over the middle light a moulded arch of its own about 8-11 px (band_m 0.09) deep rising from the posts' heads, its crown about 14 px (0.16 m) over the side lights' transoms (rise_m 0.08); a heavy bar runs on from each post's head to the head, leaning out about 23 degrees from upright (18 px across 43 px up); a concentric bar about 22 px (ring_m 0.25 m) inside the glass's edge crosses the radial bars, eleven of them where the print draws seven between the post bars and two or three outside each. The bars' sections are the kit's.

variants.head: round
variants.why_not_ordinary: a basement light: a narrow round-headed light in the raised basement, set in pairs
variants.note: A fixed round-headed basement light, one plate light, standing above grade in a raised basement: the paired arched basement lights of 1612 Prairie's photograph (T-2366).

variants.head: segmental
variants.why_not_ordinary: a basement light: one broad, low light in the raised basement under a flat segmental arch
variants.note: A fixed basement light, one plate light, broad and low under a segmental head that rises a sixteenth of its span, standing above grade in a raised basement behind its iron: the light under 1623 Prairie's arched window in the Building Budget drawing (T-2818).

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a basement light: low and wide, set in an area well below grade
variants.note: The basement light in its area well: three fixed lights, the sill below grade, the well's floor below the sill and its coping just above grade. The register's 'basement lights'.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: grouped attic lights: three small lights under one lintel, the register's 'attic grid window'
variants.note: Three small casements, four lights each, divided by stone mullions under one lintel.

variants.head: round
variants.why_not_ordinary: a leaded light: limited to stair, transom and attic positions (restrictions)
variants.note: A fixed round-headed stair light glazed in diamond quarries on lead cames: the 'limited leaded lights' of the K06 catalogue entry, in the one position it allows them most freely.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two casement lights side by side under one head, divided by a stone mullion
variants.note: Two tall casement lights under one flat head, a stone mullion between them, each glazed in small lights on bars: the ground-floor windows of 1625 Prairie's 1890 photograph (T-2752). The print does not resolve whether the bars are lead or wood, so they are the kit's moulded bars, not a leaded light; their number is the kit's, about the size of the panes the print shows.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two casement lights under a stone transom and two fixed lights over it, divided by a stone mullion
variants.note: A mullioned and transomed window of two lights, the transom about a third down: the first-floor windows of 1625 Prairie's 1890 photograph (T-2752). The bars are the kit's, as the casement pair's.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two plate-glass casement lights under a stone transom and two low fixed lights over it, divided by a stone mullion
variants.note: A mullioned and transomed window of two plate-glass lights, the transom about a third down and the lights over it low: the second storey's wide north window of 1812 Prairie's photograph (T-2889), 1.64 m across on a stone mullion about 0.18 m wide, the transom's lights about 0.45 m high over a transom bar whose foot is 0.68 m under the head. The print's small squared glazing in the transom lights is not built.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: an open loggia, not a window: two openings on a slender stone post under one head, with no frame, sash or glass, the loggia's dark depth behind them
variants.note: The open loggia in the top storey of 1801 Prairie's gabled section on 18th Street, which J. W. Taylor's c. 1895 photograph shows dark behind its balustrade, two openings on a slender post under the gable (T-1890). The print gives the loggia's place, its height and the post between its two dark openings; its depth, floor and back wall are not seen, so it is carried back the kit's backing depth in the backing's dark finish.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two plate-glass casement lights under a stone transom and two low fixed lights over it glazed in small squares, divided by a stone mullion
variants.note: k06.opening.casement_pair_transom_plate with its transom lights glazed in small squares, as 1812 Prairie's north window's are in the Levy photograph (T-3091; read at 6x, x 810-970, y 820-880 px: each transom light a lattice of small square lights, eight or so across and three or four rows in the panel the print shows bright, about 5 px or 0.055 m a light at 88.5 px a metre); built as eight by eight lights about 0.05 m square on the kit's muntins over one glass, as the fanlight lattice is (T-2819). The plate variant, which 1801 Prairie's lights also use, is unchanged.

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: two ordinary sashes and a stone mullion under one head, with a fixed transom light over each on a stone bar, glazed in small squares
variants.note: The paired sash (k06.opening.sash_paired_flat) with a fixed light over each sash on a stone bar, its glazing a row of small squares: the second storey's paired window in 1812 Prairie's south projection (T-3091, the Levy photograph at 3x, x 370-780, y 690-900 px, 92.4 px a metre at the projection's face): the sashes' heads at about y 810 (8.04 m), a heavy stone bar over them to the lights' sills at about y 793 (8.23 m), and over it in each bay a low light to about y 755 (8.64 m) whose grille the print draws as a row of small squares; the bar and the lights are laid by the record's tiers (T-2815), twelve by four lights a bay on the kit's muntins over one glass.

variants.head: round
variants.why_not_ordinary: a pictured leaded light: a fixed round-headed light a photograph shows patterned, its quarries in a field inside a border of small panes round a medallion
variants.note: 1812 Prairie's small arched window on its third storey, which the Levy photograph shows filled with a patterned light (T-3091; read at 5x, x 820-1000, y 440-620 px): an arched border of small round panes about 10-12 px (0.12 m) wide round a figured field, set deep in a dark reveal. The pattern is not legible past that, so it is built as a leaded light: a came round the field 0.12 m in, the border between cut into panes about 0.12 m long, diamond quarries in the field and a came roundel 0.2 m in radius about the head's centre, the field's medallion, standing for the figure. The reveal is the kit's deepest but one (0.2 m), the print's shadowed soffit. A leaded light outside the restriction's positions is allowed only where a picture shows one (pictured_by).

variants.head: flat
variants.why_not_ordinary: a grouped window: four casement lights under a stone transom and four fixed lights over it, divided by stone mullions
variants.note: The four-light mullioned and transomed window over the door of 1625 Prairie's 1890 photograph (T-2752). The bars are the kit's, as the casement pair's.

variants.head: segmental
variants.why_not_ordinary: a narrow light of a pair, about 0.6 m wide, under the ordinary sash's range
variants.note: A narrow two-over-two sash under a segmental head: the frontispiece's paired upper lights in 1625 Prairie's 1890 photograph (T-2752).
